entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Milton Wolff (1915-2008) emerged as a quintessential figure of American anti-fascist engagement in the 20th century, most notably as the final commander of the Abraham Lincoln Battalion during the Spanish Civil War (1936-1939). His leadership of the American volunteers within the XV International Brigade, fighting on behalf of the Second Spanish Republic against Francisco Franco's Nationalist forces supported by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, cemented his status as a symbol of international solidarity and communist commitment. Born in Bensonhurst, Brooklyn, Wolff's life trajectory mirrored the intense ideological struggles of the Modern Era, from the Great Depression to the Cold War.

Joining the Communist Party USA in 1937, Wolff volunteered for Spain, arriving in early 1938. Despite his youth and lack of prior military experience, his courage and tactical acumen quickly propelled him through the ranks. He participated in major engagements such as the Battle of Belchite and the pivotal Battle of the Ebro, where he assumed command of the Lincoln Battalion in September 1938, succeeding Robert Merriman. Under his leadership, the battalion, comprising some 2,800 American volunteers throughout the war, fought valiantly against overwhelming odds, demonstrating a fierce dedication to republican ideals before the International Brigades were withdrawn in late 1938.
